topics.title: Document Structure & Syntax
topics.summary: Learn the skeleton every HTML page is built from and how elements, attributes, nesting, and document metadata fit together.

concepts.name: Document skeleton
concepts.explanation: A modern document starts with a doctype, then an html root. The head stores metadata and resource links; the body contains content that participates in the visible page.

concepts.name: Elements and attributes
concepts.explanation: Elements give content structure. Attributes add extra information such as an id, language, URL, or input type. Attribute values should be quoted consistently.

concepts.name: Nesting and validity
concepts.explanation: Elements form a tree. Closing tags should match the element you opened, and child elements must be placed where the HTML content model permits them.

topics.title: Text, Headings & Meaning
topics.summary: Use text-level elements to communicate hierarchy and meaning instead of choosing tags only for their default appearance.

concepts.name: Heading hierarchy
concepts.explanation: Use h1 through h6 to describe section hierarchy. Avoid skipping levels simply to make text look smaller; CSS is responsible for appearance.

concepts.name: Paragraphs and phrasing
concepts.explanation: Paragraphs group prose. strong marks importance, em adds stress emphasis, and elements such as code, mark, small, sub, and sup carry specific meaning.

concepts.name: Semantics first
concepts.explanation: Semantic HTML helps browsers, search engines, and assistive technology understand content. A meaningful element is usually better than a generic div plus styling.

topics.title: Links, Images & Lists
topics.summary: Connect documents, embed meaningful images, and represent grouped or ordered information with the correct list structure.

concepts.name: Anchors
concepts.explanation: The a element creates a hyperlink. href identifies the destination; link text should explain where the link goes instead of saying only “click here”.

concepts.name: Images and alternatives
concepts.explanation: img uses src for the image resource and alt for a text alternative. Decorative images normally use an empty alt value so screen readers can ignore them.

concepts.name: Lists
concepts.explanation: Use ul when order does not matter, ol when sequence matters, and li for each item. Description lists use dl, dt, and dd for terms and descriptions.

topics.title: Forms & Basic Controls
topics.summary: Collect user input with native controls that already provide keyboard behavior, semantics, and browser features.

concepts.name: Form ownership
concepts.explanation: form groups controls that belong to one submission. action describes where data goes and method describes how it is submitted.

concepts.name: Labels
concepts.explanation: A label should be programmatically associated with its input, usually with for="id". This enlarges the clickable target and gives assistive technology a usable name.

concepts.name: Control types
concepts.explanation: input supports many types including text, email, number, checkbox, radio, date, and password. textarea and select cover longer text and predefined choices.

topics.example:
<form action="/profile" method="post">
  <label for="name">Display name</label>
  <input id="name" name="name" type="text" required>

  <label for="email">Email</label>
  <input id="email" name="email" type="email" required>

  <button type="submit">Save profile</button>
</form>
topics.challenge: Create a form with labelled name and email fields plus a submit button.
topics.hint: Give each input an id, then point the matching label for attribute at that id.
topics.solution:
<form action="/profile" method="post">
  <label for="name">Display name</label>
  <input id="name" name="name" type="text" required>

  <label for="email">Email</label>
  <input id="email" name="email" type="email" required>

  <button type="submit">Save profile</button>
</form>

topics.title: Semantic Page Structure & Accessibility Basics
topics.summary: Combine structural elements into a page that is understandable when styles are removed or when it is navigated with assistive technology.

concepts.name: Landmarks
concepts.explanation: header, nav, main, aside, and footer create useful page regions. A document should normally have one main landmark for its primary content.

concepts.name: Sections and articles
concepts.explanation: section groups a themed part of a document and typically has a heading. article is for self-contained content that could stand on its own.

concepts.name: Built-in accessibility
concepts.explanation: Start with correct native elements, meaningful headings, useful link text, alt text, and labels. ARIA is not a substitute for correct HTML.
